name: Exertional rhabdomyolysis
populations: athletes with a sudden increase in training
people with sickle cell trait or a metabolic myopathy
summary: Muscle breakdown after unaccustomed or extreme exertion (often with heat, sickle cell trait, drugs or supplements): pain, swelling, weakness, dark urine and raised CK. Suspected cases need same-day medical review.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most cases are mild and resolve without sequelae; in endurance-event reports CK and kidney markers usually returned to baseline after about 5.9 days (a pooled review with inconsistent diagnostic criteria)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Individual and guided by symptoms, CK and risk of recurrence; the guidance rests on consensus statements and case series, not trials

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Serum CK of at least 5 times normal, or a urine dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy (one sports-medicine definition); definitions vary, with CK above 1000 IU/L the other commonest cut-off

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose; blood and urine tests decide. MRI shows muscle oedema that can resemble DOMS

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 22.2 cases per 100,000 per year in US military trainees; recurrence 0.08% per person per year in a small cohort

keyFacts.label: Complications
keyFacts.value: Acute kidney injury, compartment syndrome, electrolyte abnormalities and arrhythmias

overview:
Exertional rhabdomyolysis (ER) is muscle cell injury caused by exertion, with release of muscle contents into the blood [r1,r2]. The classic picture is exercise-related muscle pain, a raised serum creatine kinase (CK) and cola-coloured urine, although early, uncomplicated cases can be subtle [r1,r3]. It follows intense, repetitive exercise, or a sudden increase in exercise in an untrained person, but also occurs in trained athletes, and heat, sickle cell trait, drugs and viral illness raise the risk [r3,r4]. Serious complications include acute kidney injury (AKI), compartment syndrome and arrhythmias [r3,r4].

The physiotherapist's role is to recognise it, stop the exercise, and arrange same-day medical assessment for CK and urinalysis, because athletes often believe it is simply delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) [r5]. After medical clearance, the physiotherapist guides a graded return. Be honest about the evidence: there is no single accepted definition [r6], diagnosis and management rest on consensus and experience, and a military practice guideline notes a paucity of evidence-based guidance for diagnosis, treatment and return to duty or play [r7]. Most cases do well; in one military series, exertional cases had less renal failure than rhabdomyolysis from other causes (odds ratio 0.45) [r8].

epidemiology.text: In a retrospective military series, 44 cases of ER occurred among 198,399 military trainees over the study period, or 22.2 cases per 100,000 per year; 63 of 177 rhabdomyolysis patients were exertional, and they had less renal failure than those with other causes (odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.22–0.95) [r8]. ER is the most common cause of exercise-related myoglobinuric acute kidney injury in athletes, although most cases are asymptomatic and resolve without sequelae [r1]. In a systematic review of endurance events (43 publications, 813 individuals, with diagnostic criteria that varied between studies), 130 people (16.39%) had ER with AKI and 96.92% of those were ultra-endurance runners; these pooled reports are not incidence figures [r9]. Case series describe ER after spinning classes in deconditioned people [r10]. In 47,944 Black US Army soldiers, sickle cell trait carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.54 (95% CI 1.12–2.12) for ER [r11].

intrinsic: Sickle cell trait: adjusted hazard ratio 1.54 (95% CI 1.12–2.12) for ER, similar to tobacco use (1.54) and a BMI of 30 or more (1.39) in a large army cohort [r11]
Lack of conditioning: strenuous, unaccustomed exercise in an untrained person [r3,r1]
Genetic susceptibility such as McArdle disease and other polymorphisms; viral infection [r4]
Recurrent episodes or a very high CK for the exercise should prompt a search for an underlying myopathy (clinical convention) [r7]
extrinsic: Strenuous, unaccustomed, prolonged and repetitive exercise, particularly in a hot and humid climate [r1,r4]
Statin use (adjusted hazard ratio 2.89, 95% CI 1.51–5.55) and antipsychotic use (3.02, 95% CI 1.34–6.82) in the same army cohort [r11]
Exercise that is improperly prescribed or used as punishment; creatine monohydrate does not appear to be a precipitating factor [r2]

mechanism.summary: ER follows exercise that exceeds what the muscle is conditioned to do, such as high-volume, repetitive or eccentric loading in a person unaccustomed to it, prolonged endurance exercise, or ordinary exercise combined with heat, dehydration, sickle cell trait, certain drugs or an underlying myopathy [r1,r4,r2]. The exact mechanism has not been clearly established, but most studies suggest a cascade of ATP depletion, failure of the sodium–potassium pump, calcium overload and sarcolemma damage that lets intracellular proteins leak into the blood [r1].
sequence: Muscle is loaded by strenuous, unaccustomed, prolonged or repetitive exercise, often with heat or another risk factor [r1].
Energy supply falls and ATP is depleted, impairing the Na+/K+ ATPase pump (proposed mechanism) [r1].
Calcium accumulates inside the muscle cell [r1].
The sarcolemma (the cell membrane) is damaged and the fibre is injured [r1].
CK, myoglobin, potassium and other cell contents leak into the circulation, causing a high CK, myoglobinuria and electrolyte disturbance [r1,r4].
The damaged muscle swells, and in a tight fascial compartment the rise in pressure can cause compartment syndrome [r3,r12].
Myoglobin filtered at the glomerulus can cause myoglobinuric acute kidney injury [r1].

variants.name: Unaccustomed resistance or eccentric exercise
variants.description: A first or much heavier session of high-repetition lowering or squatting in an untrained person; common in gym and military training [r3,r2].

variants.name: Group fitness and high-intensity classes
variants.description: Described after spinning classes in deconditioned people, with admission for rhabdomyolysis in a case series [r10].

variants.name: Endurance and ultra-endurance events
variants.description: Raised muscle and kidney markers after endurance events that usually return to baseline after a few days; AKI is rare but concentrated in ultra-endurance runners [r9].

variants.name: Heat-associated
variants.description: Exercise in intensely hot and humid environments raises the risk [r4,r1].

variants.name: Sickle cell trait, drug-related or myopathy-related
variants.description: Sickle cell trait, statins, antipsychotics and inherited metabolic myopathies such as McArdle disease increase susceptibility [r11,r4,r13].

anatomy.text: A skeletal muscle fibre is a long multinucleated cell enclosed by a sarcolemma. Inside it sit the contractile sarcomeres, mitochondria that make ATP, the sarcoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium, and enzymes and proteins such as creatine kinase and myoglobin (standard anatomy). The Na+/K+ ATPase pump in the sarcolemma maintains the ionic balance of the fibre, and failure of this system is part of the proposed injury cascade [r1]. Muscles lie in fascial compartments with limited room to swell [r12]. Myoglobin released from damaged fibres is filtered by the glomerulus and can injure the renal tubules [r1].

structures.name: Sarcolemma (muscle cell membrane)
structures.role: Contains the cell contents; damage lets CK, myoglobin and potassium leak into the blood [r1]

structures.name: Na+/K+ ATPase and the energy supply
structures.role: Maintain ionic balance; ATP depletion and pump failure lead to calcium accumulation (proposed) [r1]

structures.name: Sarcoplasmic reticulum and intracellular calcium
structures.role: Calcium excess is part of the proposed injury cascade [r1]

structures.name: Muscle compartment and fascia
structures.role: Limited space for swelling; raised pressure can cause compartment syndrome [r12,r3]

structures.name: Kidney (glomerulus and tubules)
structures.role: Filter myoglobin, which can cause myoglobinuric acute kidney injury [r1]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Skeletal muscle breakdown occurs normally with exercise, followed by repair and adaptation; ER occurs when strenuous, unaccustomed, prolonged and repetitive exercise, particularly with other risk factors such as a hot and humid climate or sickle cell trait, produces clinically significant muscle damage [r1]. The proposed cascade is depletion of adenosine triphosphate, impaired Na+/K+ ATPase function, intracellular calcium accumulation, sarcolemma damage and release of intracellular proteins and other substances into the blood [r1]. The exact mechanism has not been clearly established [r1].

The release produces the clinical picture. CK rises in the blood, myoglobin appears in the urine and can cause acute kidney injury, and electrolyte abnormalities and arrhythmias can follow [r4]. Swelling of damaged muscle within a closed compartment can also cause acute exertional compartment syndrome with rhabdomyolysis, which needs emergency fasciotomy [r12]. CK also rises after ordinary strenuous exercise, so its value as a marker of damage is debated, and normal upper limits differ by ethnicity, age and sex [r14].

structures.name: Muscle fibres
structures.effect: Sarcolemma damage and leak of CK, myoglobin and potassium; severity ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening [r1,r4]

structures.name: Kidney
structures.effect: Myoglobinuric acute kidney injury in the most severe cases; 130 of 813 individuals (16.39%) in pooled endurance-event reports had ER with AKI, mostly ultra-endurance runners (not an incidence figure) [r9,r1]

structures.name: Fascial compartment
structures.effect: Swelling and raised pressure can cause compartment syndrome with neurovascular compromise; foot drop was the presenting sign in one case [r12]

structures.name: Heart and electrolytes
structures.effect: Electrolyte abnormalities and arrhythmias can complicate severe cases [r4,r3]

muscles.name: Damaged muscle groups
muscles.effect: Pain, swelling, tenderness and weakness out of proportion to usual soreness, often in the muscles that did the unaccustomed work (clinical convention) [r5].

muscles.name: Compartment muscles
muscles.effect: Tense swelling and pain on stretch if a compartment syndrome develops [r12].

muscles.name: Recovering muscle
muscles.effect: Repair and satellite-cell regeneration, with strength returning over weeks; adaptation protects against later bouts (standard teaching; compare DOMS) [r1].

cellular.description: ATP depletion and impaired Na+/K+ ATPase function, with calcium accumulation [r1].
Intracellular proteins and other substances are released into the blood [r1].
Myoglobin is filtered at the glomerulus, with a risk of AKI; electrolyte disturbance and arrhythmia can occur [r1,r4].
Muscle and kidney markers usually returned to baseline after about 5.86 days in the systematic review of endurance sport; this pooled figure came from studies with different criteria [r9].
Repair, regeneration and graded reconditioning; the pace is individual and guided by symptoms and CK [r1,r5].

systems.effect: Myoglobin-related acute kidney injury; ER is the most common cause of exercise-related myoglobinuric AKI in athletes [r1].
Muscle swelling can cause compartment syndrome [r12,r3].
Heat and humidity raise the risk; dehydration and heat illness may coexist (clinical convention) [r1,r4].
Sickle cell trait and metabolic myopathies such as McArdle disease increase susceptibility [r11,r4].

grading.system: Mild versus severe rhabdomyolysis (systematic-review recommendation; no universal grading)

grades.description: Acute muscle weakness, myalgia and muscle swelling with CK above 1000 IU/L or more than 5 times the upper limit of normal [r6].
grades.prognosis: Most cases are asymptomatic or mild and resolve without sequelae [r1]

grades.description: As above with measured myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury [r6].
grades.prognosis: 130 of 813 individuals (16.39%) in pooled endurance-event reports had ER with AKI, mostly in ultra-endurance runners; these are pooled reports, not an incidence [r9]

grades.description: Tense compartment with pain on stretch and neurovascular change, in addition to rhabdomyolysis; managed surgically [r12].
grades.prognosis: Delay risks irreversible muscle and nerve damage [r12]

timeframes.summary: Symptoms usually appear within hours to days of the exertion (clinical convention). In endurance-event reports, CK and kidney markers usually returned to baseline after about 5.9 days [r9]. The return to training is individual and has no validated time frame [r5,r7].

healing.description: Muscle damage and leak of cell contents; symptoms, dark urine and high CK appear (clinical convention) [r1]
Fluid therapy within the first 6 hours is advised; markers typically return to baseline after about 5.9 days in endurance reports [r15,r9]
Cessation of activity and relative rest during clinical recovery [r1]
Staged and individual; guided by symptoms, CK and risk of recurrence (clinical convention) [r5,r1]

milestones.label: Same-day CK and urinalysis
milestones.note: CK at least 5 times normal, or a urine dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy, confirms the diagnosis in one sports-medicine definition [r5]

milestones.label: Intravenous fluids started
milestones.note: Preferably within the first 6 hours after muscle injury [r15]

milestones.label: Markers back to baseline (endurance reports)
milestones.note: About 5.86 days in the pooled review [r9]

milestones.label: Medical clearance for light activity
milestones.note: A clinical convention; individual and set by the treating doctor [r5,r7]

milestones.label: Return to normal training
milestones.note: A clinical convention; criteria-based, not time-based [r5]

timeframes.returnToSport: Individual and criteria-based, usually over weeks (clinical convention). It follows medical clearance, resolution of symptoms and normalisation of CK and kidney function, and an assessment of the risk of recurrence. The guidance rests on consensus statements, a military practice guideline and case series, not on trials [r5,r7,r1].

symptoms: Muscle pain that is more severe than usual soreness, with swelling and weakness, in the muscles that did the unaccustomed work [r5,r3]
Cola-coloured or dark urine (myoglobinuria), which may be absent in mild cases [r4,r1]
Early uncomplicated cases can be subtle, and the athlete often thinks it is DOMS [r3,r5]
Reduced urine output, nausea, malaise or fatigue (clinical convention)
Severe cases: palpitations or breathlessness from electrolyte disturbance, or confusion with heat illness (clinical convention) [r4]
signs: Swollen, tender, firm or tense muscles, with pain on contraction and on stretch [r5]
Weakness out of proportion to the apparent injury (clinical convention)
Tense compartment, pain on passive stretch, altered sensation or foot drop if compartment syndrome develops [r12]
Dark urine on direct inspection (clinical convention)

subjective: Exercise history: type, volume and novelty of the session, eccentric or repetitive work, whether it was used as punishment, and time since onset [r5,r2]
Environment and hydration: heat and humidity, fluid and food intake, sleep, concurrent illness [r1,r4]
Medicines and substances: statins, antipsychotics, stimulants, supplements (creatine is not a precipitant), alcohol and drugs [r11,r2,r4]
Susceptibility: sickle cell trait, family history of muscle disease or previous episodes of dark urine or severe soreness [r11,r4,r13]
Symptoms: pain compared with usual DOMS, swelling, weakness, urine colour and volume (ask the patient to look at the next sample) [r5,r4]
Red-flag screen: palpitations, confusion, severe swelling, sensory change, and any possible compartment syndrome (clinical convention)
observation: Swelling of the affected limb or muscle group compared with the other side
Urine colour on inspection if a sample is available [r4]
General appearance: distress, sweating, heat intolerance or signs of dehydration (clinical convention)
palpation: Tenderness and firmness of the muscle bellies, comparing sides [r5]
Tension of each compartment and pain on passive stretch, which indicate a possible compartment syndrome [r12]
Distal pulses and capillary refill (clinical convention)
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive range of motion of the adjacent joints, noting pain and swelling limits
Do not force range or stretch a swollen muscle (clinical convention)
strength: Test the affected muscle groups gently; weakness out of proportion to pain is a concern (clinical convention)
Record a baseline for later comparison; avoid maximal testing while the diagnosis is open (clinical convention)
neuro: Sensation and motor function distal to the swelling, including dorsiflexion and great toe extension, because compartment syndrome can present with foot drop [r12]
Reflexes and neurological screen to exclude other causes (clinical convention)
functional: Gait, stairs and sit-to-stand; the ability to walk without marked pain (clinical convention)
Observe whether pain and swelling out of proportion to the effort prevent normal tasks

specialTests.name: Urine dipstick and microscopy (arranged by a doctor)
specialTests.procedure: A dipstick test of urine, followed by microscopy if positive for blood.
specialTests.positive: A dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy confirms the diagnosis in one sports-medicine definition; a urine or serum myoglobin is more definitive when quickly available. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources read.

specialTests.name: Serum creatine kinase (CK) (arranged by a doctor)
specialTests.procedure: Blood test, repeated to follow the trend.
specialTests.positive: CK at least 5 times normal confirms the diagnosis in one sports-medicine definition [r5]; a systematic review recommends CK above 1000 IU/L or more than 5 times the upper limit of normal with the clinical syndrome for mild rhabdomyolysis [r6]. Accuracy figures for predicting AKI (pooled sensitivity and specificity from traumatic and disaster rhabdomyolysis, not exertional cases) are listed here as indirect evidence; CK alone had only fair discrimination.

specialTests.name: Compartment assessment (palpation and passive stretch)
specialTests.purpose: Screen for acute exertional compartment syndrome
specialTests.procedure: Palpate each compartment for tension and passively stretch the muscles, with a neurovascular check.
specialTests.positive: Tense swelling, pain on passive stretch and neurovascular change; diagnosis is clinical and can be supported by direct pressure measurement [r12]. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources read.

clinicalRules.name: CK at least 5 times normal or dipstick positive for blood with no red cells
clinicalRules.description: A sports-medicine definition for confirming ER in a patient with exertional muscle pain, swelling and weakness, with myoglobin more definitive when available [r5].

clinicalRules.name: Definitions vary
clinicalRules.description: A systematic review of 614 papers found that a definition was stated in 231 (37.6%), most often with a CK cut-off: more than 5 times the upper limit of normal in 22.9% and above 1000 IU/L in 27.7% of the 231; the review recommends CK above 1000 IU/L or more than 5 times the upper limit with the clinical syndrome for mild rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobinuria and AKI for severe [r6]. An endurance-sport review used CK above 5000 IU/L for ER [r9]. Quote the definition when you quote a number.

outcomeMeasures.name: Serum CK trend
outcomeMeasures.use: Medical monitoring of recovery and a guide to return to activity [r1,r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: Creatinine, electrolytes and urinalysis
outcomeMeasures.use: Medical monitoring for kidney injury and electrolyte disturbance [r1,r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain (0–10), swelling and urine colour diary
outcomeMeasures.use: Daily symptom tracking during recovery and graded return (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Strength (dynamometry) and functional tests
outcomeMeasures.use: Track recovery against the other side (clinical convention)

imaging.modality: Blood and urine tests (not imaging; medical)
imaging.findings: Raised CK, myoglobinuria, creatinine and electrolyte changes [r5,r1]

imaging.indication: Uncertain cases, or to exclude a muscle tear or other structural injury
imaging.findings: Muscle oedema can resemble DOMS, which shows diffuse oedema without fibre discontinuity; rhabdomyolysis is listed as a mimic on imaging, so correlate with CK and clinical findings [r17]

differentials.name: Delayed-onset muscle soreness
differentials.distinguishing: Soreness that typically develops 24 to 72 hours after unaccustomed or intense eccentric exercise, with no systemic features; in ER, pain, swelling and weakness are more severe, urine may be dark and CK is much higher [r17,r5].

differentials.name: Acute compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Tense compartment, pain on passive stretch and neurovascular change, sometimes with foot drop; can coexist with ER and needs emergency surgery [r12].

differentials.name: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Reproducible exercise-induced pain that settles within minutes of stopping, with no systemic features or myoglobinuria (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Calf or other muscle strain
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden onset of focal pain during a specific effort, with a palpable defect or bruising; no diffuse swelling, dark urine or systemic upset (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Exertional heat illness
differentials.distinguishing: Raised core temperature with confusion or collapse; may coexist with ER, and heat is a risk factor for it [r1,r4].

differentials.name: Drug- or statin-related myopathy and inherited metabolic myopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Statins and antipsychotics increase the risk of ER [r11], and metabolic myopathies such as McArdle disease cause recurrent episodes [r4]; recurrent or low-threshold ER should be investigated.

differentials.name: Viral myositis or other infection
differentials.distinguishing: Preceding viral illness can raise the risk of ER [r4]; fever and systemic illness favour infection (clinical convention).

redFlags: Dark or cola-coloured urine, or reduced urine output, after exertion: same-day emergency assessment for myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury [r4,r1].

Severe muscle pain, swelling and weakness out of proportion to the exercise, particularly in the first days after unaccustomed or extreme exertion: stop exercise and arrange same-day medical review with CK and urinalysis; do not wait to see whether it settles [r5,r3].
Tense compartment, pain on passive stretch, sensory change, pallor or foot drop: emergency, because acute exertional compartment syndrome can coexist with rhabdomyolysis and needs surgery [r12].
Confusion, collapse, hot skin, palpitations, chest pain or marked weakness: emergency, for heat illness, electrolyte disturbance or an arrhythmia [r4,r3].

Recurrent episodes, an unexpectedly high CK for the exercise, or known sickle cell trait, statin or antipsychotic use: arrange medical evaluation for an underlying cause before any return to hard exercise [r11,r4,r7].
Do not give vigorous massage, stretching or a hard training session as treatment while ER is possible (clinical convention).

management.principles: ER is a medical problem first. Management is cessation of physical activity, relative rest during clinical recovery and early, aggressive fluid replacement, with inpatient monitoring for kidney function, electrolytes and compartment syndrome in more severe cases [r1,r7]. The physiotherapist's job is recognition, referral and a later graded return. A military practice guideline addresses outpatient versus inpatient care, discharge criteria, recurrence risk and rehabilitation, but the evidence is limited and consensus based [r7]. There are no controlled trials of return-to-exercise programmes, so staged progression is a clinical convention [r5,r3].

medical.name: Same-day assessment, CK, urinalysis and renal function
medical.description: Confirm the diagnosis and risk-stratify; blood and urine tests decide outpatient versus inpatient care [r5,r7].

medical.name: Early intravenous fluids
medical.description: A systematic review of 27 studies concluded that intravenous fluids should be started as soon as possible, preferably within the first 6 hours, at a rate that keeps adult urine output at 300 mL/h or more for at least the first 24 hours; eight investigations found that delayed fluids increased the risk of AKI. No controlled study compared volumes or fluid types, and most studies were not of exertional cases [r15].

medical.name: Sodium bicarbonate and mannitol
medical.description: No evidence supported sodium bicarbonate with or without mannitol as superior to fluids alone; use bicarbonate only to correct systemic acidosis and mannitol only to maintain urine output despite adequate fluids [r15].

medical.name: Monitoring and treatment of electrolytes, kidney function and arrhythmia
medical.description: Severe cases can have renal failure, electrolyte abnormalities and arrhythmias and need admission and monitoring [r4,r10].

medical.name: Fasciotomy for acute exertional compartment syndrome
medical.description: Emergent fluid resuscitation and fasciotomy were required in a high-level athlete with compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis; diagnosis is clinical and can be supported by pressure measurement [r12].

medical.name: Risk assessment for recurrence
medical.description: Review sickle cell trait status, medicines and possible metabolic myopathy; a military guideline addresses identifying and assessing athletes at risk of recurrence [r7,r13,r4].

physio.name: Recognise, stop exercise and refer the same day
physio.description: Stop the session, avoid further loading, and arrange CK and urinalysis rather than treating it as DOMS [r5,r1].

physio.name: Cessation of activity and relative rest during medical recovery
physio.description: Cessation of physical activity and relative rest are mainstays of treatment [r1].

physio.name: Education on fluids, symptoms and when to seek care
physio.description: Explain the warning signs (dark urine, reduced urine output, worsening swelling) and how to return safely (clinical convention) [r4,r5].

physio.name: Staged return to exercise after medical clearance
physio.description: Return to play after recovery is influenced by associated risk factors and is guided by signs, symptoms and CK levels; the athlete is risk-stratified before deciding when and under what conditions to return [r1,r5]. There are no controlled trials, so it rests on consensus and case series [r3,r7].

physio.name: Screen for modifiable risks and plan conditioning
physio.description: Review heat exposure, hydration, medication and the rate of progression of training; build exercise tolerance gradually [r2,r4].

physio.name: Exercising through symptoms or using exercise as punishment
physio.description: Improperly prescribed exercise, or exercise used as punishment, is a recognised cause of ER [r2]; do not push through symptoms.

physio.name: Treating as DOMS with massage, deep stretching or a heavy session
physio.description: Athletes often believe ER is simply DOMS [r5]; vigorous massage or loading while the diagnosis is open is not supported (clinical convention).

physio.name: Return to full training by calendar alone
physio.description: Return is guided by signs, symptoms and CK levels, not by days [r1,r5].

education: Rhabdomyolysis is muscle breakdown. It is different from normal soreness: it can injure the kidneys, so dark urine or severe swelling after exercise needs same-day medical care.
Stop the session if the pain, swelling or weakness is much worse than you expect, and tell someone.
Drink to thirst and avoid starting very hard training suddenly, particularly in heat. Build up over weeks.
After an episode, return to exercise gradually with medical clearance and keep an eye on your urine colour and symptoms.
Tell your doctor about statins, antipsychotics or supplements, and about any family history of sickle cell trait or muscle disease.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation starts only after medical clearance and follows symptoms, CK and risk of recurrence, not dates. The staged plan below is a clinical convention built from consensus guidance; no trial has compared return-to-exercise programmes [r5,r7,r3]. Ask the doctor for CK and kidney-function targets before each step, review urine colour and symptoms the next day, and step back after any recurrence of swelling, severe pain or dark urine. Doses are conventions, not prescriptions from a trial.

stages.name: Medical recovery and relative rest
goals: Maintain normal daily activity within comfort
precautions: No exercise until a doctor clears it [r1,r7]
Dark urine, worsening swelling or pain, or reduced urine output: urgent medical review
Avoid vigorous massage or stretching of swollen muscle (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Gentle ankle pumps and walking around the house
exercises.dosage: 5 min every 1–2 hours while awake, pain-free
exercises.cues: Easy movement only; no resistance or fatigue

exercises.name: Symptom, hydration and urine-colour diary
exercises.cues: Record pain, swelling, urine colour and fluid intake

exercises.name: Education session on warning signs and risk factors
exercises.cues: Agree who to call and when

progressionCriteria: Doctor has cleared activity and CK is normal or clearly falling (medical decision)
Swelling and pain settling, normal urine colour and normal kidney function
Able to walk normally around the home without symptoms

stages.name: Light activity and re-introduction
stages.timeframe: Typically the first 1–2 weeks after clearance
goals: Restore everyday movement and walking tolerance
precautions: Use low intensity, short duration and no heat or dehydration
Stop if pain, swelling, weakness or dark urine returns
No eccentric or high-repetition work yet (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Easy walking
exercises.dosage: 10–20 min, once or twice a day, conversational pace

progressionCriteria: No recurrence of swelling, severe pain or dark urine for at least 24–48 hours after each increase
CK remains normal or low on the doctor's schedule

stages.name: Low-load strength and aerobic progression
precautions: Increase one variable at a time and allow 24–48 hours to judge the response
Avoid exercise in heat and humidity
Keep sessions well below the level that caused the episode

exercises.name: Bodyweight squat, limited depth
exercises.dosage: 2 × 8–10, twice a week, slow lowering avoided
exercises.cues: Stand up smoothly; stop well short of fatigue

exercises.name: Stationary cycling or easy jog
exercises.dosage: 15–30 min, 2–3 times a week at easy intensity
exercises.cues: Keep the intensity conversational; fluids and cool environment

progressionCriteria: Strength and function back to about 80% of the other side or pre-episode level (clinical convention)
No symptoms or dark urine after sessions
Doctor agrees that CK and kidney function allow progress

stages.name: Progressive loading and return to full training
goals: Return to full training volume and intensity
precautions: Increase volume by small steps and avoid a sudden jump in eccentric work
Keep a flare-up plan and a low threshold for medical review
Take extra care in heat and when taking statins or antipsychotics

exercises.name: Split squat
exercises.cues: Controlled lowering with gradual load increase

exercises.name: Single-leg balance and step-down
exercises.cues: Low step, slow lowering introduced gradually

exercises.name: Interval running or training-specific work
exercises.dosage: Short intervals, building weekly, once or twice a week
exercises.cues: Keep volume well below the original episode and increase by no more than about 10% a week (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Heat-acclimatised sessions
exercises.cues: Fluids available and a buddy system; stop if unwell

progressionCriteria: Full-volume training completed without symptoms, swelling or dark urine
CK remains normal after sessions on the doctor's schedule
Athlete understands risk factors and warning signs, and a monitoring plan is in place

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria exist for ER. Return is guided by symptoms, CK and risk of recurrence, after medical clearance [r1,r5]
No dark urine, swelling or unusual pain at rest or after training sessions
CK and kidney function normal on the doctor's schedule
Strength and function close to pre-episode or the other side (about 90%; clinical convention)
Risk factors reviewed: heat, hydration, medicines, sickle cell trait and possible myopathy, with recurrent or unexplained episodes investigated [r13,r4,r7]
Gradual build-up of volume with a monitoring plan and an agreed low threshold for medical review
tests: CK and renal function on the doctor's schedule
Strength testing against the other side or baseline
Graded sport-specific tolerance sessions with 24–48 hour symptom review

prognosis: Most cases are asymptomatic or mild and resolve without sequelae [r1]. In a military population, exertional cases had a lower rate of renal failure than other causes of rhabdomyolysis (odds ratio 0.45), and among 22 followed for a mean of 31.2 months there was 1 recurrence (0.08% per person per year); that was a small retrospective cohort in young, fit trainees [r8]. In endurance-event reports, muscle and kidney markers usually returned to baseline after about 5.9 days, but severe cases with AKI occur and the long-term kidney effect of repeated ER and AKI is not known [r9]. Complicated cases with compartment syndrome can cause irreversible muscle and nerve damage if treatment is delayed [r12]. Prognostic and return-to-play guidance rests on consensus and case series [r3,r7].
prevention: Progress exercise gradually and avoid sudden large increases in volume, particularly unaccustomed eccentric or repetitive work in untrained people [r3,r1].
Do not use exercise as punishment or prescribe it improperly; exercise testing and prescription should follow professional standards [r2].
Acclimatise to heat and humidity and keep fluids available [r1,r4].
Review medicines and risk factors: statins and antipsychotics, sickle cell trait, viral illness, drug and alcohol use [r11,r4,r13].
Teach athletes to recognise the warning signs and stop early: severe pain, swelling, weakness and dark urine [r5,r4].
Creatine monohydrate does not appear to be a precipitating factor, so it is not a reason to avoid it for this purpose [r2].
clinicalPearls: Dark urine plus a swollen, weak, painful muscle after unaccustomed exercise is same-day medical care, not DOMS. Athletes often mislabel ER as DOMS, so ask about urine colour [r5].

Always quote the CK definition. A systematic review found that more than 5 times the upper limit of normal and above 1000 IU/L were the commonest cut-offs, and endurance studies used above 5000 IU/L [r6,r9].
CK alone is only a fair predictor of AKI (pooled AUC 0.73, from traumatic rhabdomyolysis), so judge the whole picture: urine, kidney function, hydration and symptoms [r16].
Ask about statins and antipsychotics. In a large army cohort their hazard ratios for ER (2.89 and 3.02) exceeded that of sickle cell trait (1.54) [r11].
Return to exercise rests on consensus and case series, not trials. Be open about that, document the plan and use a low threshold for review [r3,r7].
Remember compartment syndrome: foot drop and a tense compartment after hard exercise are an emergency [r12].

captions.text: An untrained person starts a very hard session with many repetitions.
The thigh muscles work again and again, lengthening under load.
Heat, dehydration, sickle cell trait, some drugs or an underlying myopathy raise the risk.
The muscle is pushed past what it is conditioned to do.
Pain, swelling and weakness are worse than normal soreness.
Zooming into the working muscle. The drawing is schematic.

actions.text: Fibres fail: the cell membrane is damaged
CK and myoglobin leak into the blood
Swelling in a tight compartment: compartment syndrome risk

captions.text: The muscle belly is doing far more work than it is used to.
Repeated, lengthening load stretches the active fibres.
Fibres are injured and their membrane leaks. This is more than DOMS-type micro-damage.
CK and myoglobin escape into the blood. Myoglobin can injure the kidney.
The muscle swells and becomes inflamed, painful and weak.
In a closed compartment, pressure can rise and squeeze the vessels and nerves.
Dark urine, severe swelling or a tense compartment need same-day medical care.
Healthy muscle: ordered sarcomeres in a fibre with an intact membrane.
Contraction: the fibres produce force and use ATP.
Overload: repeated lengthening load strains the fibre. Energy supply and ion pumps start to fail (proposed).
Disruption: calcium builds up, the membrane is damaged and the contents leak out.
Inflammation: immune cells arrive and clear debris. CK and myoglobin are in the blood.
Satellite cells activate to repair the damaged fibres.
Regeneration: the fibres recover over weeks, and the return to exercise is gradual.
